about: As he pours water into the chalice of wine, the priest asks that through the mystery of this water and wine we may share in the divinity of Christ, who deigned to share our humanity. The prayer praises God, who wonderfully created the dignity of human nature and yet more wonderfully restored it.

s01.narrative: The priest makes the sign of the cross over the corporal with the paten, lays the Host on it and moves to the right side of the altar. At low Mass he pours the wine into the chalice himself, and blesses with the sign of the cross the water he is about to mix with it.

s02.translation: O God, who wonderfully created the dignity of human nature and still more wonderfully restored it: by the mystery of this water and wine, may we come to share in the divinity of Him who humbled Himself to share in our humanity, Jesus Christ, Your Son, our Lord: who lives and reigns with You in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever. Amen.

s03.narrative: In Masses for the Dead the prayer is said, but the water is not blessed.

w001.function: Vocative. The form is the same as the nominative, because “deus” has no separate vocative.

w002.function: The whole prayer is one sentence: a vocative, a relative clause saying who God is, and only then the petition.

w004.function: A genitive depending on “dignitátem” (w005): the dignity of human nature.

w005.function: One object for two verbs: he made it and he restored it.

w007.function: Cóndere is to found, to establish — the verb for founding cities, not fingere, shaping clay.

w009.function: The comparative of the same adverb as “mirabíliter” (w006). The form doubles as the neuter of the adjective's comparative. It is an adverb here because it modifies a verb.

w010.function: A contracted form of reformavísti — Latin often shortens the perfect this way (amásti for amavísti). The missal keeps the short form beside the full condidísti two words earlier.

w011.function: Here the petition begins. Everything before it was invocation.

w014.function: It qualifies the water and the wine together. The form marks no gender and the two nouns are of different genders, so none is claimed here.

w018.function: Accusative after “per” (w013). These are the words the offertory cut into the Christmas Collect.

w019.function: A genitive depending on “divinitátis” (w020). Its masculine gender comes from its referent, Christ, who is named only a few words later.

w021.function: The infinitive is the object of “da” (w011): grant us to be.

w022.function: The form is nominative as well as accusative. Accusative, because the understood subject of “esse” (w021) is an accusative us, not the dative “nobis” (w012). Con-sors is one who shares another's lot (sors).

w023.function: The second relative clause turns the petition around: we share his divinity because he took a share in our humanity.

w024.function: A genitive with “párticeps” (w029), just as “divinitátis” (w020) goes with “consórtes” (w022).

w026.function: The infinitive of fio — the verb that serves Latin as the passive of “to make”: fíeri means to become, to be made.

w028.function: With “dignátus” (w027) it makes one past-tense form of a deponent verb. On its own it means nothing here.

w029.function: Predicate after “fíeri” (w026). Pars-cápere: one who takes a part.

w035.function: This whole series of nouns is one apposition to “qui” (w023) — the name at last spoken.

w036.function: Here begins the conclusion of a prayer to the Father. Because the Son has just been named, it starts straight at “Qui tecum”, without “Per Dóminum nostrum”.

w037.function: One written word carrying two: the preposition cum stands after the pronoun, as it always does with the personal pronouns (mecum, nobíscum).

w045.function: Nominative, not vocative like “Deus” (w001): apposition to “Qui” (w036) — he who lives and reigns as God.

w049.function: A Hebrew idiom rendered word for word: ages of ages simply means for ever.
